posts.title: The 10-second phone test for your website
posts.hook: Grab your phone. Open your website. You have 10 seconds.
posts.facebook:
Grab your phone. Open your website. You have 10 seconds.
Web design and local search in Gainesville: https://ka-performancefl.com/?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=2026-09-26-2

Your customers run this test every day without thinking about it. Run it yourself this weekend, two seconds per check:

1. It loads fast. Turn off Wi-Fi and open your site on cell data. A blank screen or a spinner sends people back to the search results.
2. You can tap to call. Tap your phone number. If it does not start a call, that call goes to someone else.
3. Your hours are easy to find. From the first screen, can you tell if you are open right now?
4. You can read it in the sun. Step outside and read your first paragraph at arm's length. Light gray text and tiny type fail here.
5. The book or contact button is obvious. Without scrolling, point at the button that gets someone in touch with you.

Failed one? We fix these. Save this for your next site check.

Visit https://ka-performancefl.com/?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=2026-09-26-2 or call Alex at 904-210-1071.

Your customers run this test every time they find you on their phone. Run it yourself this weekend, two seconds per check:

2. You can tap to call. Tap your phone number. If it does not start a call, you are asking a customer to copy it by hand.
3. Your hours are easy to find. From the first screen, can you tell if you are open right now? Hours in a PDF, a photo of a sign, or only on Facebook do not count.
4. You can read it in the sun. Step outside and read your first paragraph at arm's length. Light gray text and tiny type fail here.

The takeaway: anything you could not tick is costing you customers. Fix the one you failed first, then run the test again.

You get back: one pick, why it frees the most time, and the words to say no. Why it matters: every yes costs an hour somewhere, and one clear no protects the goal.

Then you decide what goes out. A two-column table: AI drafts a plan for the week, you decide what matters most. AI drafts three messages, you decide what you send, and when. posts.title: LinkedIn: Five contrast fixes you can make today
posts.hook: Your phone in the sun. Can anyone read your website?
posts.linkedin:
Your phone in the sun. Can anyone read your website?

Contrast is easy to miss on an office monitor and hard to miss outdoors on a phone. WCAG 2.2 sets the line: 4.5 to 1 for body text, 3 to 1 for large text. Every ratio in this document is computed from the real hex values.

Five fixes you can make today:

1. Light gray body text measures 2.52 to 1. A darker gray gets 7.62 to 1.
2. White text on a bright photo measures 1.39 to 1. A dark scrim behind it gets 5.55 to 1.
3. White text on a bright green button measures 2.27 to 1. A deeper green gets 5.01 to 1.
4. Placeholder text used as the label measures 1.74 to 1. Put a real label above the field.
5. Links shown by color alone measure 1.78 to 1 against the text around them. About 1 in 12 men see color differently. Underline your links.

The takeaway: run your three most used text and background pairs through a contrast checker and fix anything under 4.5 to 1. Start with buttons and form labels, where a customer is trying to act.

We measure contrast on every site we build, against WCAG 2.2 at Level AA, and we audit existing sites with real numbers, not a plugin badge.

#Accessibility #WebDesign #WCAG
posts.linkedinComment: How we audit and fix accessibility: https://ka-performancefl.com/services/accessibility/?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=2026-09-29-3
posts.repost: Fix 3 is the one I would check first: white text on a bright brand button looks fine on a monitor and measured 2.27 to 1 here. Five minutes with a contrast checker catches it.

media.alt: K&A Performance slide. Huge type: Your phone in the sun. Can anyone read your website? Five numbered color chips in gray, pale sky blue, bright green, light gray, and dark teal, with the line 5 contrast fixes you can make today. Every ratio computed to WCAG 2.2.
Fix 1 of 5: Darken your light gray body text. Before card: gray #A8A29E text on white #FFFFFF, 2.52 to 1, fails 4.5 to 1 for body text. After card: dark gray #57534E on white, 7.62 to 1, passes.

Fix 2 of 5: Put a scrim behind text on photos. Before card: white headline on a pale sky blue #C9DDEA, 1.39 to 1, fails even the 3 to 1 large text line. After card: a 60 percent #221C15 scrim darkens the sky to #65696A, and the white text measures 5.55 to 1, passing 3 to 1 and 4.5 to 1.

Fix 3 of 5: Check white text on your brand buttons. Before card: a white Book a visit label on a bright green #22C55E button, 2.27 to 1, fails 4.5 to 1. After card: the same label on a darker green #15803D, 5.01 to 1, passes.

Fix 4 of 5: Stop using placeholder text as the label. Before card: an email field whose only label is light gray #C4C4C4 placeholder text on white, 1.74 to 1, fails. After card: a visible Email address label in dark ink above the field at 16.86 to 1, and placeholder text in #6B6B6B at 5.32 to 1, passes.

Fix 5 of 5: Underline your links. Before card: a dark teal #134E4A link inside near black #221C15 text with no underline, only 1.78 to 1 between link and text, fails WCAG 1.4.1 use of color. After card: the same link underlined, 9.47 to 1 against white, passes.

Recap of all five fixes, each clearing 4.5 to 1: gray text 7.62, photo scrim 5.55, button 5.01, placeholder 5.32, link 9.47. We check this on every site we build. ka-performancefl.com. Call Alex 904-210-1071.

posts.title: LinkedIn: Quiz questions that measure something
posts.hook: If everyone passes your quiz, it measured nothing.
posts.linkedin:
If everyone passes your quiz, it measured nothing.

A quiz that everyone aces tells you people can read. It does not tell you whether they can do the job, and that is the whole reason the assessment exists.

Five fixes we use on every course, each shown in this document as a weak and a strong example question:

1. Test what they would do, not what they can recite. Put the learner in a scenario and ask for the next move.
2. Make every wrong answer tempting to someone. A distractor nobody picks is a free point.
3. Retire "All of the above." It rewards guessing, not knowing.
4. Ask it straight. Trick negatives test reading, not judgment.
5. Write feedback that teaches the why. "Incorrect, the answer is B" is a missed lesson.

The example questions are ours, written for a customer service course.

The takeaway: take one recall question from your current quiz and rewrite it as a short scenario with a decision at the end. Then give each wrong answer feedback that explains why it is wrong.

We design and build training content, from full courses and short modules to assessments and job aids, delivered into your own LMS. Free sample courses are on our site.

#InstructionalDesign #LearningAndDevelopment #eLearning
posts.repost: A quiz everyone passes looks great on a completion report and tells you almost nothing about the job. If you only try one of these, try fix 5: feedback that explains the why.

media.alt: Lined exam paper with a score of 100 percent circled in red pen. Headline: If everyone passes your quiz, it measured nothing. Five fixes for quiz questions that measure something, with weak vs strong examples.

Fix 1 of 5, recall vs application: test what they would do, not what they can recite. Weak example: What is the first step of our complaint process? Strong example: a customer with a damaged order cuts you off mid policy; the highlighted answer is stop, let them finish, and restate what happened.

Fix 2 of 5, distractors: every wrong answer should tempt someone. Weak example: how to greet a customer, with joke options like Ignore them crossed out in red. Strong example: you are on a call when someone walks up; the highlighted answer is make eye contact and signal you will be right there.

Fix 3 of 5: retire All of the above. Weak example: Good customer service includes, with All of the above circled as guessable. Strong example: a refund is a week late; the highlighted reply apologizes, says it is flagged, and promises an email update by Friday.

Fix 4 of 5: ask it straight, no trick negatives. Weak example: a double negative question with NOT and avoid circled in red. Strong example: an upset customer raises their voice; the highlighted answer is I can hear this has been frustrating, let's sort it out.

Fix 5 of 5: feedback should teach, not just grade. Weak example feedback: Incorrect, the correct answer is B. Strong example feedback explains that calm down can sound like their feelings are the problem, and that naming the frustration first shows you heard them.
We build training people finish. Scenario questions, real distractors, and feedback that teaches. See the samples at ka-performancefl.com/training or call Alex at 904-210-1071.

posts.title: LinkedIn: The four-line brief. Save this.
posts.hook: Copy this before your next AI request.
posts.linkedin:
Copy this before your next AI request.

When a first draft from an AI tool misses, the request is usually one line long, and the tool fills every gap with average. Four lines above the request close those gaps:

1. Who it is for. Name the reader and what is on their mind.
2. What good looks like. Length, tone, and the one thing the reader should do.
3. What to avoid. List what would make you delete the draft.
4. The format you want. Ask for the shape, and it arrives ready to use.

This document walks through a worked example of each line, a spring email for a fictional lawn care company, then puts all four on one fill-in-the-blank card you can save. It works in any AI tool.

The takeaway: before your next request, write one sentence for each of the four lines. The reader and the limits matter most, because the tool cannot guess them.

Putting AI to work inside a business is part of what we do, alongside web design, local search, and training. Our free AI lessons teach practical habits like this one.

#AI #SmallBusiness #Productivity
posts.repost: "What to avoid" is the line I never skip. One sentence of limits saves me more rewriting than anything else I put in a request.

media.alt: K&A Performance slide on a cream background: Copy this before your next AI prompt. An index card below lists four numbered lines: who it is for, what good looks like, what to avoid, the format you want. Save this post. Swipe for line 1.

Big rust numeral 1: Who it is for. Name the reader and what is on their mind. Example index card for a fictional lawn care company's spring email reads: For: past customers who booked a spring cleanup last year, busy homeowners reading on their phone. Why it matters: the reader sets the tone, the length, and what to leave out.

Big rust numeral 2: What good looks like. Describe done, or you get average. Example card reads: Good looks like: under 120 words, one ask, book a spring cleanup online, sounds like the owner, not an ad. Why it matters: the AI cannot read your standards, so say them once.

Big rust numeral 3: What to avoid. List what would make you delete the draft. Example card reads: Avoid: no discount codes, no exclamation points, do not promise dates because the schedule fills up. Why it matters: one line of limits saves you three rounds of edits.

Big rust numeral 4: The format you want. Ask for the shape, and it arrives ready to use. Example card reads: Format: a subject line under 50 characters, three short paragraphs, the booking link on its own line. Why it matters: ready to paste means ready to send.

Screenshot this: the four-line brief as a fill-in-the-blank index card. Task: the job, in one line. Then four blanks: For, who it is for and what is on their mind. Good looks like, length, tone, the one thing they should do. Avoid, what would make you delete the draft. Format, the shape you want back.
